title: A Asset for the Deadline
premise: Coral Marchetti, a traumatized interpreter who survived a massacre at a failed peace summit, has lived under witness protection for two years. When she spots the safe house's interior in a real-estate listing, she realizes someone inside the program is selling her location. Following the thread, she uncovers a plot to stage a catastrophic 'accident' at a reconciliation conference, designed to bury both her testimony and the truth about who ordered the massacre. Racing a deadline she alone knows about, Coral must decide whether to trust the one investigator who believes her, expose the conspiracy publicly, and accept that survival means stepping out of the shadows — even if it costs her the anonymity that kept her alive.
about_author: Theo Amberdale is the pen name of a former NGO field coordinator who spent a decade in conflict zones before turning to fiction. They write thrillers about ordinary people trapped inside machinery far larger than themselves.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Scrolling listings at 3 a.m., Coral recognizes her own kitchen, her own curtains, in photos of the safe house. Panic sets in as she catalogs what the images reveal: the layout, the sightlines, her. The emotional beat is the shattering of her carefully maintained illusion of safety.

chapters.title: Protocol of Silence
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She calls her handler, Voss, who dismisses it as a data error and orders her to stay put. Coral notices Voss's answers are too smooth, rehearsed. She photographs the listing before it's taken down an hour later. Beat: first crack in her trust in the program.

chapters.title: Interpreter's Ear
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Coral's POV. Two years earlier: the summit, the massacre, the phrase she translated that she's never told investigators — a coded instruction she understood too late. Beat: guilt established as the engine of her sleeplessness.

chapters.title: The Man Who Waits
chapters.summary: Investigator Dane Okafor's POV. Okafor, a disgraced federal auditor, has been quietly re-examining the summit massacre and keeps hitting sealed files. He receives an anonymous tip pointing to Coral. Beat: the second protagonist enters, motivated by institutional betrayal.

chapters.title: House Hunting
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She traces the listing to a boutique agency whose owner has one client with government contracts. Watching the agency, she spots a man photographing her building. Beat: fear sharpening into purpose — she chooses to investigate rather than run.

chapters.title: Contact
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Okafor approaches Coral; she nearly flees, but he quotes the coded phrase from her flashback — something never in any file. They agree to a fragile, distrustful alliance. Beat: reluctant belonging, the first human connection since the incident.

chapters.title: What the Photos Sold
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The listing photos were taken from inside; only program personnel had access. She builds a shortlist of three handlers with financial troubles. Voss goes silent after she leaves him a coded voicemail. Beat: the conspiracy has a shape and a face count.

chapters.title: The Reconciliation Conference
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. A high-profile follow-up summit is announced at a converted hydroelectric plant — a venue with a documented structural vulnerability. Okafor realizes an 'accident' there would kill the surviving witnesses, Coral included if she testifies. Beat: the deadline becomes concrete.

chapters.title: Tail Lights
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Someone ransacks the safe house while she's out; they take nothing but her old translation notebooks. She understands: they want the phrase she never reported. She relocates on her own terms, off the grid. Beat: severing from protection, embracing risk.

chapters.title: Three Handlers
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor works his shortlist: one dead by apparent suicide, one vanished, one — Reyes — still active and nervous. A tense interview yields a name: Meridian Group, a private security contractor with summit access. Beat: the enemy acquires an institutional body.

chapters.title: The Phrase
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral finally decodes the full instruction she half-translated two years ago: it wasn't a warning, it was a go-order. The massacre wasn't a failure of the peace process — it was its design. Beat: devastating reframe of her guilt into evidence.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Okafor and Coral infiltrate a Meridian subcontractor's office; Coral's language skills crack a cipher in shipping manifests — demolition-grade charges routed to the plant as 'stage equipment.' Beat: competence and partnership replacing isolation.

chapters.title: Voss Returns
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Voss finds her, claims he's been investigating from inside, offers extraction. Coral notices his shoes are caked in red clay — the soil around the hydro plant. She lets him believe she's coming. Beat: betrayal confirmed; Coral now plays the game.

chapters.title: Deadline Math
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Okafor cross-references the summit schedule with the shipping dates: the attack is set for the closing ceremony, eleven days out, timed to a 'routine inspection' that will explain the structural failure. Beat: the clock made explicit; stakes quantified in lives.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Wouldn't
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral tracks down the summit's surviving security chief, who confirms Meridian's role but refuses to testify, terrified. She gives Coral one thing instead: the name of Meridian's client. Beat: the cost of survival shown in another's brokenness — Coral's mirror.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The program brands Coral a fugitive; wanted bulletins with her photo flood the channels she once hid inside. Voss's voice on the radio offers her a last chance to surrender. Beat: the safety architecture fully weaponized against her.

chapters.title: Eleven Hours
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Inside the plant, posing as conference staff, Coral maps the charge placements using the manifest data. She's nearly caught by Meridian teams sweeping for her; she hides in the turbine gallery where the massacre's logic was first drafted. Beat: terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: The Client
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. The client is a coalition of officials who needed the peace process to die with the witnesses — including the architect of the witness program itself. Okafor gets the file to one honest journalist and one honest judge, hedging against his own death. Beat: justice outside the law takes shape.

chapters.title: Closing Ceremony
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The ceremony begins. Coral, spotted, forces Voss to choose between the detonation sequence and her public arrest. She begins translating the emergency announcement herself — turning the attack's cover story into a live confession broadcast. Beat: the interpreter becomes the message.

chapters.title: Detonation Interrupted
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Okafor's evidence forces the venue's evacuation on a technicality as Meridian triggers a partial charge; the reinforced wing holds, casualties minimal. Voss, exposed, tries to silence Coral and is stopped — not by agents, but by conference delegates who shield her. Beat: climax; strangers become her belonging.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Weeks later, Coral testifies in open court, translating for herself for the first time — no one between her words and the record. The program is dismantled; Meridian's client list bleeds into headlines. Beat: justice achieved through exposure, not vengeance; the price fully counted.

chapters.title: Sleep
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Coral, in a new city under her own name, falls asleep at a normal hour and wakes to morning light. A postcard from Okafor, one line: 'The house is off the market.' Beat: resolution — survival no longer means hiding; the price was paid, and she is still herself.
